An Overview of Ten Simple Rules for Reproducible Research

Ten Simple Rules for Reproducible Computational Research

Reading

  • Title: Ten Simple Rules for Reproducible Computational Research
  • Author(s): Sandve G.K., Nekrutenki A., Taylor J., Hovig E.
  • Year: 2013
  • Journal: PLOS Computational Biology 9(10): e1003285
  • https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pcbi.1003285

Review

  1. For Every Result, Keep Track of How It Was Produced


  1. Avoid Manual Data Manipulation Steps


  1. Archive the Exact Versions of All External Programs Used


  1. Version Control All Custom Scripts

Review

  1. Record All Intermediate Results, When Possible in Standardized Formats


  1. For Analyses That Include Randomness, Note Underlying Random Seeds


  1. Always Store Raw Data behind Plots


  1. Generate Hierarchical Analysis Output, Allowing Layers of Increasing Detail to Be Inspected

Review

  1. Connect Textual Statements to Underlying Results


  1. Provide Public Access to Scripts, Runs, and Results

Why are we here?

  • Beyond Morality: Reproducibility isn’t just a moral obligation to your field; a lack of tracking is a direct technical burden on you.

  • The Time-Saver: Meticulous tracking allows your future self to effortlessly apply past methods to new data or reuse code templates across separate projects.

  • The Bare-Minimum Threshold: At an absolute baseline, you must at least be able to reproduce your own results to defend your science against future questioning.

  • The Reality Check: Because any given analysis contains an exponential combination of parameters and software variables, memory will fail you. You must record details while underway.

The Core Definition

An analysis workflow is the full sequence of:

  • pre-processing,
  • script executions,
  • and post-processing required
  • to get from raw data to a final plot.

Rules 1 & 2: Eliminating Human Drift

  • The Documentation Trap: Manual logs easily drift out of sync with how an analysis was actually performed in its final iteration.

  • The Executable Solution: Write your entire workflow as a directly executable file—such as a shell script or a Makefile.

  • Ban Manual Clicks: Completely avoid manual copy-pasting or graphical format tweaks between documents. Replace mouse clicks with reproducible format converter scripts.

Rules 3 & 4: Freezing Your Software State

  • The Version Lock: Minor changes between software updates can alter data outputs or prevent code from running entirely.

  • The Virtual Machine Shield: If a program has deep operating system or library dependencies, archiving a full virtual machine image is the only viable safeguard.

  • Systematic Backtracking: If code states are not systematically tracked via Git, proving your past results weren’t the product of a transient bug becomes impossible.

Rule 5: Exposing the Pipeline’s Inner Mechanics

🔬 The Analytical Value

Quickly browsing through step-by-step intermediate output files can reveal silent logical discrepancies, catching bugs that are completely masked in final summary charts.

🛠️ The Pipeline Value

If your full project execution is long or resource-heavy, archiving standardized intermediate states allows you to re-run localized parts of the process without starting over from scratch.

  • The Audit Baseline: Storing intermediate files allows external peers to critically examine your complete pipeline logic without needing all your local executables operational.

Rules 6 & 7: Perfect Replications & Data Foundations

Rule 6: The Random Seed Mandate

Many analyses involve stochastic element randomness. To achieve an exact procedural reproduction rather than just an approximation, you must explicitly record and pass your initial random seed.

  • Isolate Visual Tweaks: Figures are modified constantly before publication. Store the raw, un-binned data separately behind your charts.

  • The Scripted Plot: If plotting in an environment like R or Python, preserve the exact code chunk used to render the graphic. You can then execute quick aesthetic axis or color shifts via code without re-running long statistical computations.

Rule 8: Generating Hierarchical Output

  • The Summary Illusion: Final publication charts and tables represent heavily compressed, summarized distributions (like a single mean value along a curve).

  • The Inspection Obligation: Fully validating your findings requires you to inspect and verify the granular, detailed sub-values underlying those summaries at least once.

  • The Hypertext Blueprint: The authors advocate for structuring output as HTML hypertext.

  • The Click Connection: This creates an intuitive data ecosystem where readers can simply click a summarized data point to follow a link directly to its raw, underlying source matrix.

Rule 9: Connecting Textual Claims to Result IDs

  • The Separation Flaw: Throughout a project, interpretations live in separate text files, emails, or markdown notes, while data results live on a local workstation or cluster server.

  • The Matching Failure: Tracing which exact version of an analysis supports a specific paragraph or conclusion becomes highly error-prone as the project’s data pool scales.

  • The Early Bind: Force yourself to embed explicit file paths, hash tags, or analysis result IDs directly into your notes the exact moment you draft an interpretation.

  • Literate Documents: Leverage integrated processing engines (like Sweave, Quarto, or interactive workflow environments) to weld your live data results directly inside your descriptive text files.

Rule 10: Providing Public Access to Your Workflow

“Making reproducibility of your work by peers a realistic possibility sends a strong signal of quality, trustworthiness, and transparency.”

— Sandve et al. (2013)

  • The Minimum Material: Submit your core data frames and raw source code scripts as mandatory supplementary online files upon publication.

  • The Review Advantage: Exposing your full workspace infrastructure increases reviewer trust, accelerates editorial turnaround times, and boosts your project’s future citation metrics.

  • The Open Stance: Always remain prepared to openly answer peer requests for deep architectural or parameter pipeline metrics.

Discussion Time

Scenario 1

You’ve been working on a lab report for the past few days. Today is the deadline and you open your computer at 2:00 AM to finish the lab report. You see four files in your folder: analysis.R, analysis_final.R, analysis_definitive.R, and analysis_actual_final_v4.R.

  • Which file contains your actual, correct work?

  • What file naming approach is better:

      1. Incremental numbering?
      1. Date-stamping?
03:00

Remind students that if they can’t tell which file is the real one, a computer definitely can’t.

A better approach would be to use a version control tool like Git.

Scenario 2

Your teammate creates a breathtaking, beautifully styled bar chart for a group presentation. However, when the professor asks to see the 10,000 raw data points that generated the third bar, your teammate sweats and says, “Uh, it’s on my old laptop.”

  • Can a highly styled chart have any actual academic value?

  • Should losing access to raw files be treated as an acceptable, relatable accident or as a fundamental failure of professional data management?

  • Should the student be accused of data fabrication?

05:00

A pretty chart without raw data trails isn’t science; it’s just creative writing/coding. There is not a lot of academic value in a breathtaking, highly styled chart if the baseline data supporting it cannot be produced on demand.

The burden of proof. In some professional environments, an inability to instantly back up a specific visual claim with its underlying numbers looks less like a mistake and more like data fabrication.

Scenario 3

A student keeps a beautiful, 100-page handwritten leather notebook. She tracks every single mouse click, every copy-paste action, and every manual data-cleaning step she performs in Excel with flawless precision.

  • Is the student’s work reproducible?

  • What alternative approaches can the student use?

  • Is there any value in (or place for) hand-written notes?

05:00

A beautifully kept manual record still fails the core requirement of being an “executable description” that a computer can run and scale.

Manual copy-paste actions and Excel mouse clicks introduce silent, untraceable human errors that version control cannot catch. We should prefer automated scripts that require zero human intervention to repeat.

There is immense value in handwritten notes and manual approaches, but only as a sandbox for human thought, not as the final pipeline for data execution.

The “Why” vs. the “How”: Code is excellent at tracking how a calculation is done, but it is terrible at explaining why you chose to do it. A handwritten notebook is a cognitive sandbox. It is where a researcher maps out messy conceptual logic, sketches potential workflows, and processes failures before writing a single line of script.

Also, a handwritten notebook is a cognitive sandbox. It is where a researcher maps out messy conceptual logic, sketches potential workflows, and processes failures before writing a single line of script.

Scenario 4

You spend three weeks testing a hypothesis on a dataset. Your code is perfect, your pipeline is automated, but the results prove your hypothesis is completely, totally wrong. Your script yields a massive “dead end.”

  • Did your hypothesis fail, or did you?

  • Did you just waste 3 weeks of work?

  • Would you still share your work in a public repo?

05:00

  1. Did your hypothesis fail, or did you? It’s important to separate the quality of your code from the behavior of nature.
    Also, an automated “failed” experiment is actually a massive engineering success.

  2. Did you just waste 3 weeks of work? The danger of deleting your dead ends: What happens to the scientific community when researchers hide their failures, forcing the next person to waste weeks re-testing the exact same wrong idea.

  3. Would you still share your work in a public repo? Submit and store it with the exact same reproducibility standards as a success, because documenting “blind alleys” saves future researchers from wasting time on the same mistake.

Scenario 5

Your script runs a 4-hour simulation on a large dataset, processing everything live in temporary memory to output a final summary paragraph. When your professor spots an anomaly and asks to see the data right after the initial filtering step, you realize nothing was saved along the way.

  • What are some advantages of a single “all-or-nothing” live run?

  • What are some disadvantages of saving intermediate steps?

05:00

Disadvantages of a pipeline that only saves the final answer: impossible to troubleshoot, audit, or verify when a bug or anomaly inevitably appears in the middle.

Discuss the massive waste of time and computational energy that happens when you treat data analysis as a single “all-or-nothing” live run instead of caching milestones.

Debate the engineering trade-off between consuming hard drive space to store temporary milestone files versus consuming hours of processing time to re-run scripts.

Better to transform a 4-hour pipeline into a modular, flexible workflow that can be paused, inspected, and restarted at any point.

Poll

Be completely honest: When cleaning a dataset or fixing file formatting issues for an assignment, how often do you rely on manual copy-pasting, visual cell edits, or find-and-replace clicks instead of writing a code script?

  1. 100% Code Scripted: I never touch the raw file manually; every transformation is written in a reproducible script lines.

  2. The Hybrid Scramble: I try to script, but if a deadline is tight, I secretly open Excel to quickly delete bad rows or copy-paste columns.

  3. Purely Manual: I do almost all data formatting visually using trackpad movements and mouse clicks because it feels faster.

  4. The “I Don’t Track It” Stance: I change cells casually as I work and completely lose track of what I manually edited by the end of the day.

Poll

  • You notice a minor discrepancy in an analysis plot you generated three weeks ago.
  • You need to backtrack to the exact code state that produced that specific figure.
  • What is the reality of your current local file system?

  1. Perfect Provenance: Every single script modification is systematically frozen in a timestamped Git commit hash; I can jump back in seconds.

  2. The “Folder Vault” Cluster I have copies named script_v1.R, script_v2_fixed.R, and script_final_REAL.R. It will take hours of manual guessing.

  3. The Overwrite Abyss: I continuously modify a single file without saving historical backups. That past code state is permanently gone.

  4. The Cloud Illusion: I assume my automatic background Google Drive/Dropbox sync will save me, even though it doesn’t track execution states.

Poll

  • You run a classmate’s stochastic simulation script on your machine using identical data inputs.
  • Because they forgot to pass a static random seed, your output values are approximately close (e.g., 84.2% accuracy) but not exactly equal to their published value (84.5%).
  • What is your scientific verdict?

  1. Acceptable Replication: Close enough is good enough for computational science; minor stochastic fluctuations don’t undermine the core theory.

  2. Unverifiable Black Box: An approximate match is a failure; without an exact mathematical match via a random seed, I cannot verify if the pipeline is truly bug-free.

  3. Indifferent Stance: I assume the difference is caused by our different operating system kernels or processor architectures anyway, so a seed won’t fix it.

Poll

  • Think about how you write lab reports, group notes, or draft research paragraphs.
  • Where do your conceptual interpretations live relative to the raw output data files that support them?

  1. Fully Welded Documents: I use integrated dynamic document tools (like Quarto or Jupyter Notebooks) so my text and live data logic are locked together natively.

  2. The Absolute Path Blind Bind: I manually type hardcoded server folder paths (e.g., /Users/name/Desktop/run_3) inside a separate Microsoft Word document.

  3. The Total Disconnect: My data lives in a folder on a local server, and my interpretations live entirely in casual emails, Slack chats, or scrap paper notes.

Poll

You are preparing to submit your finalized computational report. What is your group’s stance on providing full public access to your custom scripts and intermediate datasets?
